opus-5.5.text:
I think it's very possible, and honestly that's one of the things I'm most excited about. Right now, the way most people use video data is almost an afterthought. You pretrain some visual representation on Ego4D or YouTube, and then you hope it transfers when you fine-tune on robot data. It helps a bit, but it's not a fundamental shift. I don't think that means the data is useless. I think it means we haven't found the right way to extract what matters from it.

If you look at a YouTube video of someone cooking or fixing a bike, there's an enormous amount of information there: what the task structure is, what objects matter, how things move, what contact looks like, what the intent is. What's missing is the action in the robot's own embodiment. There's no joint torque, no gripper command, and the human hand is very different from a parallel-jaw gripper. So the question is whether we can find an intermediate representation that's shared between humans and robots, so the gap stops mattering so much.

There are a few directions that I think are promising. One is to predict things that both humans and robots can express, like object motion, hand or end-effector trajectories, or 3D flow in the scene, and then have a much smaller embodiment-specific layer that maps that into robot actions. Another is world models: learning how the world evolves from video, so the robot can imagine outcomes and plan, rather than just imitating. And a third, which my lab has spent a lot of time on, is treating human data as a first-class data source. That means collecting egocentric human demonstrations with the right sensing so they're closer to robot data, and co-training on both, instead of treating human video as a side dish.

The way I think about it is that YouTube is like the internet text of robotics. Language models didn't work because someone hand-labeled everything. They worked because next-token prediction happened to be an objective that could absorb all that raw data. For robotics, we haven't found our next-token prediction yet, the objective that naturally soaks up passive video and turns it into physical competence. I don't think it's going to be exactly the same recipe. Physical interaction has things like force and contact that video just doesn't show you. So you'll probably always need some real robot data to ground things. But if the paradigm shifts so that video provides most of the "what" and "why," and a small amount of robot data provides the "how," that changes the economics of robot learning completely. I'd be surprised if we don't see real progress on that in the next few years.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, and I want to start by being honest that I'm somewhat skeptical, but hopeful.

The dream is obvious, right? There are billions of hours of people doing things with their hands on YouTube. Cooking, assembling furniture, fixing bikes. If you could just pour that into a model the way we poured the internet into language models, you'd have a robot that knows how the physical world works. And every few years someone says, this is it, now we have the architecture that unlocks it.

The reason it hasn't worked yet is that the gap between watching and doing is much bigger than it looks. When you watch a video, you get the visual outcome of a behavior, but you don't get the actions. You don't get the forces, the contacts, the little corrections someone makes when the screw doesn't catch. And crucially you don't get the embodiment. A human hand is not a parallel-jaw gripper. So even if you learn something from the video, there's this translation step, and historically that step has eaten most of the benefit.

That said, I don't think the problem is fundamentally that the data is useless. I think the problem is that we've been asking it to do the wrong job. We kept trying to extract policies from video, like actions directly. I think the more realistic version is that video teaches you the things that are embodiment-agnostic. What objects afford, how tasks decompose into steps, what a successful outcome looks like, what the world does when you push on it. That's world knowledge, not motor control. And then you use a comparatively small amount of real robot data to ground that knowledge in a specific body.

So when people ask about a better paradigm, that's what I'd point to. Not a model that reads YouTube and outputs torques, but a model where video gives you the prior, the representation, maybe a learned world model or a reward signal, and the robot data does the last mile. The recent progress in video generation actually makes me more optimistic about this than I was a few years ago, because those models clearly learn something about physics and object permanence, even if they also hallucinate.

The part I'd push back on is the idea that scale alone solves it. In language, the data and the output are the same modality. In robotics they're not. So I think we'll need to be more deliberate about what we're trying to learn from video, rather than hoping the next bigger model just figures it out.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s very possible. When we say YouTube data isn’t useful for robot learning, we’re usually making that statement relative to a particular way of training robots. If your method needs an observation paired with an exact robot action, then a human video is missing a lot of what you need.

But that doesn’t mean the information isn’t there. You can see what people are trying to accomplish, how they break a task into steps, and how objects change as they interact with them. The question is how to connect that information to what a robot can actually do.

Maybe the right paradigm is to learn those broader structures from video, and use robot experience to ground them in actions. You would still need interaction to learn things that are difficult to see, like forces or contact. But you might need much less robot data than if you were learning everything from scratch.

So I’m optimistic about the possibility. I think we should distinguish between ‘this data doesn’t work with our current method’ and ‘this data has nothing useful to teach us.’ Those are very different claims.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s very possible. When we say YouTube data isn’t useful for robot learning, we may really mean that we don’t yet have the right way to use it. A video doesn’t give you the robot’s actions or the forces involved, but it does show how tasks unfold, how objects interact, and what success looks like.

The question is how to connect that information to actions a robot can actually take. Maybe we learn a lot of that structure from video, then use robot experience to ground it in a particular body. I’m open to a better paradigm making that work. The important test is whether watching those videos actually helps a robot learn a new task with less interaction.
